tip: A short, cheerful children's piece: a perfect first piece to read. Keep the left hand light and even.

tip: A lullaby: rock gently in the left hand and let the melody float.

tip: A march up the grand staircase. Steady tempo, crisp rhythm.

tip: Three layers at once: bass, chord and melody. The left hand leaps from bass to chord on every bar; learn it alone until the leap is automatic.
The same layered texture as No. 1 in a warmer color. Keep the left hand gentle and the melody singing.
Darker and slower. The left hand carries bass and chords; the right hand has only the melody.
Written without bar lines in the original. The left hand is a steady bass-and-chord pattern; keep the grace notes in the melody loose and late.
A question without an answer: let each phrase hang. The left hand alternates bass and chord.
src: Paris : Rouart, Lerolle & Cie., 1913. Plates R.L. 9884-9886 & Cie. Possibly scanned from the Dover reprint.

tip: Hypnotic left-hand chords under a winding melody. Count steadily even where the music seems to float.
src: Paris : Rouart, Lerolle & Cie., 1913. Plates R.L. 9884-9886 & Cie. Possibly scanned from the Dover reprint.

tip: Eight short phrases in a mazurka rhythm. Shape each one as a single breath.
The left-hand chords change one note at a time. Learn them alone, notice which note moves, and keep them soft and even under the melody.
The melody is in the left hand. Make it sing; the right-hand repeated chords stay light.
A chorale of heavy chords. Voice the top line and keep the pulse broad and steady.
A strange, bleak prelude: a slow melody over a creeping left-hand pattern of intervals.
Grand and solemn. Count the dotted rhythms precisely against the triplets.
The repeated A-flat is the rain. Keep it soft and even while the melody sings above it.
Wide left-hand arpeggios almost throughout: ideal preparation for the later nocturnes.
Melancholy and flexible. Bass on beat 1, lighter chords on 2 and 3, so the melody can lean.
Practice every ornament slowly and in rhythm before fitting it in. Left hand steady, right hand free.
Light and quick. Build speed with short bursts; the running right hand must stay relaxed.
Four against three throughout. Learn each hand alone, then put them together very slowly; speed comes last.
Slow and grave, like a frieze. Balance the chords so the top line is always heard.
Flowing triplets and two-against-three. Practice those spots hands separately, counting, then together very slowly.
Playful and light. Keep the triplet figures crisp and the hands relaxed.
src: Paris: Durand et Schoenewerk, n.d.[1891]. Plates D.S. 4395-96

tip: Count the 9/8 carefully in the opening; the rhythm is subtler than it sounds. In the flowing middle, move the arm with the arpeggios instead of stretching.
Built on the whole-tone scale. Keep the low B-flat pedal point soft and let the textures blur gently.
Learn the quiet outer sections first. For the climax, use arm weight and release; never push.
Three layers: bass, rippling middle and melody. Practice each layer alone, then in pairs.
A march in repeated chords. Practice wrist staccato slowly and keep the forearm relaxed.
